## {#today .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.todaymeta}
A one-day course on data tools, in four parts of 90 minutes, on the housing-audit case
:::

:::: {.todaybox}
::: {.nonincremental .fs-85}
1. Credibility and the toolchain – why the tools matter, and what each of them does
2. R and the IDE – the paper, the data, and a first session in R
3. Data management and the reproduction – from the public file of a study to a reproduced result
4. The report and its record – a Quarto report, a clean run, and the versions of a project
:::
::::

::: {.todaytake .fs-85}
You leave with R code that reproduces a published result, a report whose numbers come from that code, and a map of the toolchain
:::

::: {.todaymeta}
Work along in the browser lab, solo or in pairs, or in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.) if you have installed the workspace
:::

::: notes
Welcome – good to have you here. A full day in four parts of ninety minutes, and today the tools are in the foreground. The first part says briefly why any of this matters, with the evidence on how often published findings survive being checked, and then takes the toolchain apart layer by layer. The second introduces the case, an experiment in which a thousand emails asked housing authorities in the United States how to apply for public housing, and gives you a first session in R on its data. In the third you manage those data, from the file that the original authors published to the columns that an analysis needs, and the R work reaches its target: you reproduce one of five published reanalyses of the claim, whichever you choose. In the fourth that result goes into a report whose numbers come from the code, and we look at how a project keeps its versions.
:::
